notes.quote: אֶת־זִמְרָן֙ וְ⁠אֶת־יָקְשָׁ֔ן וְ⁠אֶת־מְדָ֖ן וְ⁠אֶת־מִדְיָ֑ן וְ⁠אֶת־יִשְׁבָּ֖ק וְ⁠אֶת־שֽׁוּחַ
notes.text: See how you used commas and conjunctions in similar lists of names in Genesis 22:22, 24.

Some languages have a specific word such as “left” or “willed” that means to give something as an inheritance. In that time and culture, a father would give his children their inheritance before he died. or [And Isaac inherited all that Abraham owned]

notes.quote: וַֽ⁠יְשַׁלְּחֵ֞⁠ם & בְּ⁠עוֹדֶ֣⁠נּוּ חַ֔י קֵ֖דְמָ⁠ה אֶל־אֶ֥רֶץ קֶֽדֶם
notes.text: The Hebrew word **Kedem** means “east” and refers to the region east of Canaan and the Dead Sea. Consider whether it is best in your language to transliterate (copy) the Hebrew name or to translate the meaning. or [but after that he sent them to the east country] or [and after that he made them move away to the east country]
The idiom **full** refers to a long life that was blessed by God. or [After he had lived a long and blessed life]
The Hebrew text has two different ways to refer to the Hittites; compare the phrase here with verse 9 where a single Hebrew word is used to refer to this people group.
Be consistent here with how you spelled **Beer Lahai Roi** in Genesis 24:62.

notes.quote: וְ⁠אֵ֣לֶּה שְׁמֹתָ֔⁠ם בְּ⁠חַצְרֵי⁠הֶ֖ם וּ⁠בְ⁠טִֽירֹתָ֑⁠ם שְׁנֵים־עָשָׂ֥ר נְשִׂיאִ֖ם לְ⁠אֻמֹּתָֽ⁠ם
notes.text: The Hebrew words for **settlements** and **camps** overlap in meaning. Both refer to temporary or permanent places where people settled, surrounded by some sort of wall or fence. Also, many translations have “princes” here instead of “rulers,” but these Ishmaelite rulers were not actually sons of a king. or [Each of them became the ruler of a tribe that was named after him, and each tribe had its own villages and tent settlements]

Be consistent here with how you spelled **Havilah** in Genesis 2:11; 10:7, 29 and **Shur** in Genesis 16:7; 20:1. The name **Shur** means “wall.” The Wilderness of Shur may have been named after a city or fortification named Shur that was located near the eastern border of Egypt (Genesis 16:7).

notes.topic: The meaning of this idiom is uncertain
notes.text: The meaning of this idiom is uncertain. Or it could mean: (2) “They settled in the presence of all their relatives.”; (3) “He died in the presence of all his brothers.” or [Ishmael died while all his brothers were still alive]
We have already heard about much of Isaac’s history in previous chapters; now we are told even more.
The Hebrew text has **they** here, which probably refers to Esau’s parents and may include people in general after his parents named him.
Consider whether or not to include the meaning of Esau’s name in the text or in a footnote.
If you decide to include the meaning of Jacob’s name in the text or in a footnote, make sure it matches the way you translate **grabbing** earlier in this sentence.

According to verse 34, this stew (or thick soup) was made out of lentils, which are a type of bean; it may also have had pieces of meat in it. Consider what is the best way in your language to introduce the first event in this episode (following the background information in verses 27–28). or [One day when Jacob was making some stew]

The Hebrew word for **exhausted** means Esau was very tired (perhaps even feeling faint) from his hunting or work, as well as hungry and thirsty from lack of food. Some languages have an idiom for this that fits well here. or [and he was weak and hungry] or [very tired and hungry]
Frequently in the Hebrew text, this phrase has a general meaning and does not refer to someone specific. or [they called him]
You could include the meaning of **Edom** in your translation or in a footnote so that it is clear why Esau was given that name.
Also see how Hebrews 12:16 is translated, which refers to the same event. or [that he was selling his firstborn-son-rights to him in exchange for the stew]

notes.quote: וְ⁠יַעֲקֹ֞ב נָתַ֣ן לְ⁠עֵשָׂ֗ו לֶ֚חֶם וּ⁠נְזִ֣יד עֲדָשִׁ֔ים
notes.text: Consider again how you translated **stew** in verses 29 and 34. Lentils are small, round, flat, reddish-brown legume seeds that grow inside a pod (similar to peas or beans). If lentils are not known in your area, you could describe them as “a type of legume called lentils.” or [Then Jacob gave Esau some of the lentil stew with some bread]
